title: Minimize the Maximum Adjacent Element Difference
statement:
The integer array `nums` has gaps: every entry equal to `-1` is unknown. Pick two positive integers `x` and `y` (they may be equal) one time only, then overwrite each `-1` with one of them; different gaps, and different slots of the same gap, may receive different values from the pair. Known entries stay as they are.

After filling, look at the absolute difference of every pair of neighbouring entries and take the largest. Return the smallest value this largest difference can have over all choices of `x`, `y` and of which one goes into each slot. When `nums` has no `-1`, the answer is simply the largest neighbouring difference.
constraints: nums[i] is -1 or an integer in [1, 10^9]
notes:
## Intuition

Only the known values next to a gap matter for choosing `x` and `y`; call the smallest `low` and the largest `high`. If the answer is `d`, some chosen value is within `d` of `low` and some within `d` of `high`. Moving them inward as far as allowed, to `low + d` and `high - d`, keeps every neighbour they could reach and brings them closer together, so fixing `d` fixes the pair and testing `d` is one greedy pass. A bigger `d` never hurts, so binary search finds the smallest that works. (Labelling every slot `x` or `y` and solving each labelling also works, in exponential time.)

## Approach

1. Scan `nums`. Known neighbours give `fixed`, the largest difference no choice can change. Each run of `-1` becomes a gap `[before, after, canSwitch]`; a gap at an end of the array copies its single neighbour into both sides, and `canSwitch` says it has two or more slots.
2. Track `low` and `high` over all gap neighbours. With no gaps, return `fixed`.
3. `fits(d)` sets `x = low + d` and `y = high - d`. A gap is fine if one value is within `d` of both sides, or if it has room to switch, each side is near some value, and `y - x <= d`.
4. Binary search `d` between `fixed` and `max(fixed, high - low)`, which always fits.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, -1, 10, 8]`: `fixed = max(1, 2) = 2`, one gap `[2, 10, false]`, so `low = 2` and `high = 10`. The search runs over `[2, 8]`. `d = 5` fits (`x = 7` is within 5 of 2 and 10), `d = 3` does not (`x = 5`, `y = 7` are each 5 away from one side), `d = 4` fits with `x = 6`. The answer is `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log V), where V = 10^9: one scan, then about 30 checks over the gaps.
- Space: O(n) for the list of gaps.

## Pitfalls

- A single-slot gap cannot switch, so one value must be close to both sides.
- The answer can never go below `fixed`; start the search there.
- A gap at either end of the array has only one neighbour; copying it to both sides lets the same test handle it.
- An array of only `-1` has no gaps with neighbours: the answer is 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `fixed` | largest difference between two neighbouring known values |
| `gaps` | each run of `-1` as `[before, after, canSwitch]` |
| `end` | last index of the current run of `-1` |
| `low`, `high` | smallest and largest value next to a gap |
| `d` | candidate answer tested by `fits` |
| `x`, `y` | the pair tried for that `d` |
| `left`, `right`, `mid` | binary search bounds on the answer |
